metadata.title: Reproduction package: A Greedy Load-Balancing Approach to Automated Multi-Resource Scheduling for Environmental Sampling Operations
metadata.description:
First public release of the reproduction package for the paper: "A Greedy Load-Balancing Approach to Automated Multi-Resource Scheduling for Environmental Sampling Operations" (Chen, Tseng, Chiu, Lai; under review).

Reproduces: CV by strategy (manual/greedy/random/first-fit); manual same-day double-booking diagnosis and feasible-subset CV; per-staff Wilcoxon; day-block bootstrap; a constraint-respecting permutation test; and the greedy-vs-exact (CP-SAT) optimum for the personnel subproblem.

Run: python3 -m pip install -r requirements.txt && bash run_all.sh (Python 3.9+, NumPy, SciPy, OR-Tools).

Data: no confidential data included; make_synthetic_data.py fabricates a data set with the same schema (illustrates the method's qualitative behaviour, not the paper's exact figures). The real LIMS extract is available from the corresponding author on reasonable request. License: MIT.

metadata.title: Convex temperature damage to global food 1 production, concentrated in drought years and 2 summer-dry economies
metadata.description:
Data and reproduction package for "Convex temperature damage to global food production, concentrated in drought years and summer-dry economies" (Leirvik, Nature Food).

This deposit contains the processed analytical dataset, all intermediate data files, and the analysis scripts needed to reproduce the results, tables and figures in the manuscript.

The study analyses a balanced country-year panel of 141 countries over 1961–2023, built from CRU TS v4.08 climate data, the World Bank Food Production Index and ESG indicators, and FAOSTAT crop yields, together with CMIP6 SSP scenario projections. It estimates a convex temperature damage function for national food production growth, tests where damage falls across the growth distribution and across countries, and evaluates whether a compound heat–drought channel is detectable at annual national resolution.

Contents. The archive root holds the merged analytical dataset (df_bf.xlsx, 9,024 × 98), the CRU-derived climate panel, the World Bank and FAOSTAT inputs, the country-specific bridging regressions used for the SSP projections, the projection objects, and the causal-machine-learning outputs (causal forest, X-learner and Bayesian causal forest country-level treatment effects). code/ contains a script that rebuilds the cached analysis workspace from the deposited data, plus the scripts generating the event-study coefficients, the projection gap tests and their decomposition, the level-versus-growth tests, the specification sensitivity analysis, the bootstrap standard errors and the crop-level marginal effects. derived/ retains the estimates those scripts write, so published numbers can be checked without re-running anything. CODEBOOK.md documents every variable, including the standardisation conventions, which differ between the panel regressions and the causal forest.

Reproducibility. R ≥ 4.5 (results produced under 4.5.1); key packages fixest, grf, quantreg, DIDmultiplegtDYN. Random seeds are fixed and recorded: the causal forest uses seed 42, the heterogeneity-robust event study and all bootstraps use seed 20260725. Every other estimate is deterministic. README.md gives the directory layout the scripts expect and the order in which to run them.

Provenance. CRU TS v4.08 (University of East Anglia CRU/NCAS, Open Government Licence); World Bank Open Data (CC BY 4.0); FAOSTAT via Our World in Data (CC BY 4.0); CMIP6 via the KNMI Climate Explorer. Derived files and scripts are released under CC BY 4.0.

metadata.title: Rainfall-product choice alters normalized storage-reliability estimates in Ambovombe, southern Madagascar: Reproduction package
metadata.description:
This record archives the complete computational reproduction package for the study “Rainfall-product choice alters normalized storage-reliability estimates in Ambovombe, southern Madagascar.”

Study scope

The analysis covers Ambovombe commune in the Androy Region of southern Madagascar. The dissolved study polygon covers 477.8 km². Three daily rainfall products were analyzed over the common period from January 1, 1995, through December 31, 2024, comprising 10,958 consecutive days:

- Direction Générale de la Météorologie Rainfall Estimate, DGM RFE;
- Climate Hazards Infrared Precipitation with Stations, CHIRPS2 Final;
- ERA5-Land.

The products were treated as equal-rank rainfall representations. No product was designated as an observation or accuracy reference because no continuous local daily gauge record covering the complete study period was available for direct evaluation.

Scientific purpose

The package supports the calculation and attribution of differences in normalized storage-reliability thresholds among the three rainfall products. The analysis separates:

- differences in long-term mean effective rainfall;
- differences in monthly input trajectories;
- differences in the daily allocation of rainfall within months.

The attribution combines product-wise mean scaling, a 3 × 3 recombination of monthly totals and intramonth daily profiles, 1,999 paired intramonth randomizations, and conditional factorial decomposition.

Package contents

- SM1 provides the detailed methods, equations and references.
- SM2 contains the exact executed analysis, validated daily rainfall series, analysis script, configuration, intermediate outputs, logs, manifests and quality-control results.
- SM3 contains eight publication graphics, plotting data, captions and the figure-generation script.
- SM4 contains six manuscript tables, machine-readable table data and the table-generation script.
- SM5 contains the three QGIS rainfall collectors and the Ambovombe study polygon.
- SM6 provides portable execution paths, dependency versions, provenance records, expected results, geographic files, licensing information and independent verification scripts.

Reproduction

Two reproduction paths are documented:

1. exact reproduction from the three validated polygon-level daily series retained in SM2;
2. recollection of DGM RFE, CHIRPS2 Final and ERA5-Land from their respective public source services using the SM5 collectors and the archived study polygon.

The three canonical analysis inputs use the schema:

"date, unit_code, rainfall_mm, rainfall_volume_m3"

Archived execution checks

The completed execution passed:

- 28 mandatory synthetic tests;
- 204 quality-control checks;
- zero warnings;
- zero failed checks.

The central time-reliability storage thresholds were 65.0, 67.5 and 122.5 days of demand for DGM RFE, CHIRPS and ERA5-Land, respectively. The corresponding volume-reliability thresholds were 62.5, 65.0 and 120.0 days.

Monthly-total source accounted for approximately 99.7% of the observed time-threshold variation and 99.5% of the observed volume-threshold variation. Its sum of squares exceeded those of daily-profile source and interaction in all 1,999 generated daily orders for both reliability metrics.

These values are normalized diagnostic thresholds and are not direct dimensions for a physical reservoir.

Data and licensing

The polygon-aggregated validated daily analytical series are retained in SM2 for exact reproduction. Native provider grids, provider caches, service credentials and authentication tokens are not included.

Original code is licensed under the MIT License. Original documentation, the study geometry and author-created derived outputs are licensed under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International. Third-party rainfall and boundary products remain attributed to their respective providers.

metadata.title: Windowed-MTP: B200 reproduction package
metadata.description:
Windowed-MTP — B200 reproduction package v1.0.0

Initial public release. Reproduction artifact for the paper "Windowed-MTP: Removing the Full-Context Draft-KV Tax at Million-Token Context" (arXiv:2607.21535). Reproduces the core result: applying a StreamingLLM-style sliding window + attention sink to the built-in MTP/NEXTN draft's attention (leaving full-attention verification intact) cuts the per-decode-step cost by +28% to +44% at 1M context across three architectures, while preserving acceptance length and the target's verified output.

What's included

  • SGLang patch (patch/windowed_mtp.patch) — windowed draft attention + compact draft-KV ring buffer, plus drop-in num_stages-tunable Triton extend/decode kernels.
  • Seeded, in-repo RULER generators (src/gen_ruler.py) — byte-reproducible 1M-token inputs (niah_multiquery_enum, fwe_enum, cwe); no dataset license, no network.
  • Run/config scripts (run/, setup/, config.env) — one-command headline sweep and single-point runs; Docker and enroot/pyxis+SLURM supported.
  • Benchmark harness + steady-state TPOT/AL parser (src/bench_sglang_mtp.py, src/parse_gt.py).

metadata.title: Ambovombe 2030 reproduction package: capacities and rainwater harvesting
metadata.description:
Version 1.0.0 reproduction package for the manuscript “Ambovombe water supply in 2030: capacities and rainwater harvesting”.

This record contains the numerical inputs, source locators, CSV exports, Python reproduction script, generated tables and figures, detailed hydraulic results, and machine-readable verification report used for the quantitative results reported in the companion manuscript.

Running:

python scripts/reproduce.py

recreates the outputs directory and returns:

VALIDATION: PASS

The validation report records 58 successful verification checks.

The package reproduces the calculations used for:

1. population and water-demand scenarios for Ambovombe at the 2030 horizon, using requirements of 20, 30, and 50 L/person/day;
2. empirical P20, P50, and P80 design rainfall derived with Hazen plotting positions from the 1995–2024 DGM RFE rainfall series;
3. required roof areas and shared-catchment areas for rainwater collection;
4. cyclic monthly storage requirements;
5. comparison of documented AES, Efaho, F015, Antanimora, rainwater-harvesting, and reuse pathways;
6. 432 Efaho head-loss and pumping-energy scenarios.

For the reference scenario of 30 L/person/day, P80 rainfall, and a roof collection efficiency of 0.85, the package reproduces a projected 2030 demand of 2,934.978619 m³/day, a P80 annual rainfall of 567.015662 mm/year, a required roof area of 222.271523 ha, and a cyclic monthly storage requirement of 218,499.622388 m³.

Interpretive scope:

- documented or nominal capacity is not treated as delivered water service;
- calculated collection areas and storage volumes are requirements, not inventories of available assets;
- the Efaho corridor is an order-of-magnitude control corridor, not an execution alignment;
- quantity calculations do not establish drinking-water quality or sanitary compliance;
- reuse is not quantified when the required input information is unavailable.

The archive includes README.md, LICENSE.md, CITATION.cff, MANIFEST_SHA256.txt, requirements.txt, source_map.csv, declared input files, the reproduction script, generated outputs, and validation_report.json. The accompanying PDF provides execution instructions, package contents, reference results, scientific scope, and licensing information.

Copernicus DEM attribution:

The Efaho elevation profile was produced using Copernicus WorldDEM-30 © DLR e.V. 2010-2014 and © Airbus Defence and Space GmbH 2014-2018 provided under COPERNICUS by the European Union and ESA; all rights reserved.

Third-party and institutionally supplied inputs remain subject to the rights and conditions of their original providers, as documented in LICENSE.md and source_map.csv.

metadata.title: Reproduction Package for the ICSE 2027 submission "Precision Exchange and Reuse across Verifiers"
metadata.description:
Reproduction Package for the Paper “Precision Exchange and Reuse across Verifiers”

Abstract

This artifact is a reproduction package for the paper “Precision Exchange and Reuse across Verifiers” which has been submitted to ICSE 2026.

It consists of all executables, input data and results required to reproduce the experiments. In particular, it also contains the original results of the paper and a way to generate the macros, csv’s, and plots used in the paper from it.

We run the experiments using 2 cores and 15 GiB of memory for either 15 minutes (CPU time) or 30 minutes.

A full reproduction of the experiments requires roughly 500 days of CPU time. For demonstration purposes, a subset of tasks has been selected which should take at most 1 day to complete and will likely finish sooner. To test that everything is working as intended, we provide a configuration that terminates within ~30 minutes.

Requirements

All the tools in the artifact have been compiled for a x86 architecture, so it will in general not be possible to run them on an ARM chip. In addition the artifact, when unpacked takes around 40 GiB or disk space, and requires at least 3 cores and 16 GB of memory to run it.

For the smoke-test 3 cores and at least 5 GB of memory are required.

Contents

This artifact contains the following items which are relevant for the ICSE 2027 submission. Other files are relevant only for exploratory experiments, which are described under further-experiments:

  • README.md: This file.
  • benchmark-defs/*.xml.template: Templates to generate benchmark definition files for running the experiments using BenchExec.
  • tasks/*.xml: Sets of tasks
    • tasks/all.xml: All tasks used to produce the results in the paper.
    • tasks/subset.xml: Subset of the tasks used in the paper.
    • test/test.xml: One task used only for the smoke test of the Artifact.
  • doc: Some documentation about the project in order to make it fully reusable also for other purposes.
  • data-analysis: Scripts and definitions to produce the plots used in the paper. Additionally they also generate the macros used to generate the tables in the paper.
  • benchmark-utils/*: Benchmarking utils
    • local_config.sh: File with parameters for BenchExec
    • check_configured.sh: File which checks that BenchExec is set up correctly
  • Makefile: Makefile to run the experiments.
  • results-paper: Raw results of the experiments presented in the paper.
  • results-smoketest: Raw results of the smoke-test executed on the CAV 26 VM.
  • License.txt: License information for the artifact.
  • sv-benchmarks: The SV-COMP26 benchmarks. Unnecessary files have been removed to make the artifact smaller.
  • Tools can be found in the tools directory.
    • CPAchecker: CPAchecker at commit (removed for anonimity) in the folder cpachecker.
    • Slowbeast: Slowbeast at commit (removed for anonymity) in the folder slowbeast
    • Theta: Theta at commit (removed for anonymity) in the folder theta

This ReadMe contains the following sections to help the user to reproduce the experiments:

  • TL;DR: A quick guide to reproduce the experiments and analyze the data.
  • Environment: Describes the environment in which the artifact was tested and can be run.
  • Experiments: Describes how to execute the experiments and generate the results.
  • Results: Describes where the results can be found and how to analyze them.
  • Known Issues: Describes known issues when executing the artifact.
  • Reuse and Further Experiments: Documentation on how to reuse the artifact for other purposes and other experiments which are already possible.

TL;DR

  1. Extract the files in the provided ZIP archive to an arbitrary directory and open a terminal inside it.
  2. Execute the script ./setup_vm.sh if you are using the CAV 26 VM to set up the environment correctly, and install all required dependencies. This will restart the VM once.
  3. Set the environment variables:
    • source benchmark-utils/local_config.sh: to setup the parameters to run inside the VM
  4. Choose one of the following sets of tasks to run:
    • make setup-benchmark: Reproduce all results in our paper on your machine (takes about 500 days of CPU time, requires 2 cores and 16GiB of RAM per run). We strongly discourage from running this inside a VM.
    • make setup-subset: Reproduce the results on a representative subset of our tasks (takes ~1 day of CPU time).
    • make setup-test: Smoke test the VM and the setup (takes ~30 min).
  5. Run make verify-all to run the verification of all the tools with all their configurations to export the witness based precision files.
  6. Run make reverify-all to reverify all the tasks using the produced witness-based precision files.
  7. Run make process-results to process the produced results in order to get human readable results. They can be found in the results/tables directory. The CSV files used to generate the plots in the paper can be found in the results/output directory.

Environment

To run the artifact BenchExec, Python >= 3.8, Java >= 21, and Clang == 14 are required.

Inside a clean VM running Ubuntu 24.04, please see the documentation of the respective tools for installation hints. A non-exhaustive list of required packages: * CPAchecker: Java 21 * Slowbeast: Clang 14 * Theta: Java 21, libgomp1, libmpfr6

NOTE: We assume that all of the following commands are executed from inside the root directory of the artifact!

NOTE: This artifact requires a large amount of disk space (around 20 GiB) to store all the benchmarks, tools, and results.

Experiments

Setup

Run source benchmark-utils/local_config.sh (needs to be repeated every time a new shell is opened).

Benchmark Selection

Depending on your available resources you can select different sets of benchmarks to execute the tools on. You have the following options:

  • A quick test with a single file, which can be useful to test that the artifact is behaving as intended. To select it use make setup-test. Executing this benchmark set should take ~30 minutes.
  • A subset of the tasks used for the benchmarks in the paper. To select it use make setup-subset. Executing this benchmark set should take around 1 day.
  • The full benchmark set used in the experiments. To select it use make setup-benchmark. Executing this benchmark set will take around 500 days of CPU Time.

Running the Experiments

To run all experiments multiple targets need to be executed one after the other, their list and order can be found in the TL;DR. Each of them encompass multiple targets for the different producer and producer+consumer combinations.

All experiments are run using BenchExec in order to ensure reliable benchmarks.

Smoke Test Results

After running the target make verify-all, the output on the command line should be similar to the contents in verify-all.txt.

Afterwards when running make reverify-all, the output on the command line should be similar to the contents in reverify-all.txt.

Results

Generating the Results

Once you ran all experiments execute make process-results to generate HTML tables which contain the information used for all three claims. They can be found in the results-paper/tables directory. The output of this command should match the contents of [smokte]

These tables can be read as follows:

  • results-cpachecker-predicateAnalysis.table.html:
    This table contains the precision reuse experiments which analyze if using the precision improves the performance of the re-verification for predicate analysis.
    The columns are named after the targets: $PRECISION_CONSUMER-using-$PRECISION_PRODUCER-$EXCHANGE_TYPE.$SPECIFICATION. Where we compare the two different ways of passing precision in the $EXCHANGE_TYPE:
    1. the predmap.txt which is CPAchecker custom precision format,
    2. the predmap-C.yml which is a precision exchange file with the precision as C expressions, and
  • results-cpachecker-valueAnalysis.table.html: This table contains the precision reuse experiments which analyze if using the precision improves the performance of the re-verification for value analysis. The columns are named after the targets: $PRECISION_CONSUMER-using-$PRECISION_PRODUCER-$EXCHANGE_TYPE. $SPECIFICATION. Where we compare different ways of passing precision in the $EXCHANGE_TYPE:
    1. the witness-value.txt which is CPAchecker custom precision format of relevant memory locations, and
    2. the witness-value.yml which is a precision exchange file with the precision as C expressions representing the relevant memory locations.
  • results-slowbeast.table.html: This table contains the precision reuse experiments which analyze if using the precision improves the performance of the re-verification for predicate analysis for slowbeast. The columns are named after the targets:
    1. the predicates.yml: which is a precision exchange file with the precision as C expressions.
  • results-theta-pred.table.html: This table contains the precision reuse experiments which analyze if using the precision improves the performance of the re-verification for predicate analysis for theta. The columns are named after the targets: $PRECISION_CONSUMER-using-$PRECISION_PRODUCER-$EXCHANGE_TYPE.$SPECIFICATION. For this we only have one way of passing the precision in the $EXCHANGE_TYPE:
    1. the pred.txtwhich is a Theta custom precision format, and
    2. the pred.yml which is a precision exchange file with the precision as C expressions.
  • results-theta-expl.table.html: This table contains the precision reuse experiments which analyze if using the precision improves the performance of the re-verification for explicit state analysis for theta. The columns are named after the targets: $PRECISION_CONSUMER-using-$PRECISION_PRODUCER-$EXCHANGE_TYPE.$SPECIFICATION. For this we only have one way of passing the precision in the $EXCHANGE_TYPE:
    1. the pred.txtwhich is a Theta custom precision format, and
    2. the pred.yml which is a precision exchange file with the precision as C expressions.

To compare your results with those obtained by the experiments for the paper, we recommend comparing the HTML tables directly between those in results/tables and results-paper/tables, since all numbers used in the paper were extracted from them.

Known Issues

Warnings

Overheating

During the execution of the experiments, a warning may appear which tells us that the CPU was throttled due to overheating. This affects the time measurements in the results, but should not happen when reproducing the results outside a VM.

2024-XX-XX XX:XX:XX - WARNING - CPU throttled itself during benchmarking due to overheating. Benchmark results are unreliable!

Overlayfs

During the execution of the experiments, a warning may appear which tells us that the home directory should be given as an overlay or hidden. Currently it is not possible to do neither of those inside the TACAS23 VM due to its old overlayfs and due to not knowing the path to the folder where the artifact is being executed.

2024-XX-XX XX:XX:XX - WARNING - Home directory in container should be /home/benchexec but this directory cannot be created due to directory mode of parent directory. It is recommended to use '--overlay-dir /home' or '--hidden-dir /home' and overwrite directory modes for subdirectories where necessary.

Resource Requirements

During the execution of the experiments, a warning may appear which tells us that the resource requirements are being ignored. This only means that the resource requirements regarding CPU model are being ignored, this has no effect on the benchmarking.

Errors

Overlay

When BenchExec tries to create an overlay mount while there is a shared folder mounted inside the VM, the following error may occur:

2024-XX-XX XX:XX:XX - ERROR - Failed to create overlay mount for /home/...: invalid argument ...

In this case, the shared folder should be unmounted and the experiments should be run again.

C Groups

If BenchExec is unable to use C groups to benchmark then a restart of the VM may help make BenchExec work as intended.

metadata.title: Reproduction package — Internal erosion raises resistivity in freshwater embankment dams: a petrophysical polarity criterion and detection limits for resistivity monitoring
metadata.description:
Code, input data, and result files that reproduce every figure and table of:

Oh, S. (2026). "Internal erosion raises resistivity in freshwater embankment dams: a
petrophysical polarity criterion and detection limits for resistivity monitoring."
Submitted to Journal of Applied Geophysics.

The study shows that in the freshwater reservoirs and clayey cores of inland embankment
dams, internal erosion raises rather than lowers electrical resistivity, because most
intact-core conduction is clay surface conduction. From Waxman–Smits petrophysics it
derives a closed-form polarity criterion on a pore-water-conductivity versus
cation-exchange-capacity phase plane, reduces the data-space signature of a core defect
to a scaling law A_max ≈ 45 (D/z)^2, and embeds this in a voltage-aware error model and
per-datum detection index that yields per-mode minimum detectable defects. The framework
is tested against a reconstruction of the Älvkarleby full-scale test embankment and
against archival surveys of two operational Korean dams (Unmun salt-tracer time-lapse;
Yeongcheon control).

Contents
- Analysis and figure scripts (Python, pyGIMLi): petrophysics and Monte Carlo
  (analysis.py, paper_figs.py), data-space sweep (e1_sweep.py), 3-D confounders
  (e3_3d.py), heterogeneity Monte Carlo (e9_hetero.py), seasonal double-difference
  separability (e12_separability.py), dam-height geometry sweep (e13_geometry.py),
  mode/array detection index (e5_fieldstats.py), Älvkarleby benchmark (e10_benchmark.py),
  site error-model calibration (e8_site_error.py), robustness checks
  (e11_robustness.py, e11d_zone3d.py), field figures and re-inversion
  (f_field_figs.py, reinvert.py), and case-projection tooling (p1_project.py).
- Pre-computed result files (results/*.json), derived field-data products
  (results/field_data/*.csv, results/field_reinv/*.npy), figure captions, and the
  manuscript's nine figures.
- README.md with the full figure/table-to-script map and runtimes.

Environment: Python >= 3.11 with pyGIMLi 1.5–1.6, numpy, matplotlib, scipy.

Field-data provenance: the operational-dam analyses are provided as derived data
products. The underlying archival raw survey data (1999–2003 Korean dam-safety
campaigns) were acquired by the original investigators and are held by the originating
agencies (Korea Institute of Geoscience and Mineral Resources; K-water), available on
reasonable request. The Älvkarleby benchmark uses only values published in Norooz et al.
(2021, J. Appl. Geophys. 191:104355) and Norooz et al. (2024, J. Civ. Struct. Health
Monit. 14:1275–1294).

License: source code under the MIT License; result files and derived data products under
CC-BY-4.0.
keywords: embankment dam, internal erosion, piping, electrical resistivity tomography, ERT, detectability, anomaly polarity, Waxman–Smits, dam safety, survey design, pyGIMLi

metadata.title: Reproduction Package for the CAV 2026 submission: "SvLibChecker: A Light-Weight Tool for Software Model Checking"
metadata.description:
Reproduction Package for the Paper “SvLibChecker: A Light-Weight Tool for Software Model Checking”

Abstract

This artifact is a reproduction package for the paper “A Light-Weight Tool for Software Model Checking” which has been accepted at CAV 2026.

The CAV paper presents SvLibChecker, a light-weight tool for software model-checking which is ideal for teaching and rapid-prototyping. SvLibChecker implements nine different algorithms for software model-checking, each in around 100 LOC, and many of its algorithms perform similarly to CPAchecker’s, a state-of-the-asrt software model-checker, on the SV-COMP26 SV-LIB benchmarks.

THe artifact consists of all executables, input data and results required to reproduce the experiments. In particular, it also contains the original results of the paper and a way to generate the macros and csv’s to generate the plots in the paper from it.

We run the experiments using 2 cores and 15 GiB of memory for at most 15 minutes (CPU time).

A full reproduction of the experiments requires roughly 30 days of CPU time. For demonstration purposes, a subset of tasks has been selected which should take at most 1 day to complete and will likely finish sooner. To test that everything is working as intended, we provide a configuration that terminates within ~15 minutes.

Requirements

All the tools in the artifact have been compiled for a x86 architecture, so it will in general not be possible to run them on an ARM chip. In addition, the artifact, when unpacked takes around 700MB of disk space, and requires at least 3 cores and 16 GB of memory to run it properly. The test-set, i.e., the smoketest can be executed with 2 Cores and 6 GB of memory.

Since there are usually differences in the instructions between different CPU models, re-building the tools for the specific CPU model may be necessary. When using a VM this is taken care of by the script setup_vm.sh which compiles the tools for the specific CPU model of the VM. In case this does not work take a look at the Known Issues section for more information.

For all further requirements, please take a look at the setup_vm.sh script, which installs all required dependencies into the CAV 26 VM and sets up the environment correctly.

Contents

This artifact contains the following items:

  • README.md: This file.
  • benchmark-defs/*.xml.template: Templates to generate benchmark definition files for running the experiments using BenchExec.
  • tasks/*.xml: Sets of tasks
    • tasks/all.xml: All tasks used to produce the results in the paper.
    • tasks/subset.xml: Subset of the tasks used in the paper.
    • test/test.xml: Few tasks used only for the smoke test of the Artifact.
  • doc: Some documentation about the project in order to make it more reusable
  • data-analysis: Scripts and definitions to produce the CSV files used to generate the plots in the paper. Additionally, they also generate the macros used to generate the tables in the paper.
  • benchmark-utils/*: Benchmarking utils
    • local_config.sh: File with parameters for BenchExec
    • check_configured.sh: File which checks that BenchExec is set up correctly
    • svlibchecker-configs: Configs for SvLibChecker used for the experiments
  • Makefile: Makefile to run the experiments.
  • results-paper: Raw results of the experiments presented in the paper.
  • License.txt: License information for the artifact.
  • sv-benchmarks: The SV-Benchmarks repository with SV-LIB benchmarks in version beee8104aeee08591d8af0d5813ddfa03877bd90. Unnecessary files have been removed to make the artifact smaller.
  • Tools can be found in the tools directory.
    • CPAchecker: CPAchecker version 5bf8b77394d234a58291601b5b951dcedd9f798f.
    • SvLibChecker: SvLibChecker version 47ea213d6c15fb83dcc8b9c048ef50af9391cfe5.

This ReadMe contains the following sections to help the user to reproduce the experiments:

  • TL;DR: A quick guide to reproduce the experiments and analyze the data.
  • Environment: Describes the environment in which the artifact was tested and can be run.
  • Experiments: Describes how to execute the experiments and generate the results.
  • Smoke Test: Describes how to run the smoketest and the expected results
  • Results: Describes where the results can be found and how to analyze them.
  • Information for Reuse: Documentation on how to reuse the artifact for other purposes.
  • Known Issues: Describes known issues when executing the artifact.

TL;DR

Before starting, if you are using a VM make sure to configure it to use at least 3 cores, at least 16GiB of RAM. If you are using vboxmanage on a computer with Linux, this can be done with running VBoxManage modifyvm "MyVM" --cpus 3 --memory 16500.

  1. Extract the files in the provided ZIP archive to an arbitrary directory and open a terminal inside it.
  2. Execute the script ./setup_vm.sh if you are using the CAV 26 VM to set up the environment correctly, and install all required dependencies. This will restart the VM once.
  3. Set the environment variables:
  • source benchmark-utils/local_config.sh: if you have an overlayfs in version 1.10 or newer installed
  1. Choose one of the following sets of tasks to run:
    • make setup-benchmark: Reproduce all results in our paper on your machine (takes about 15 days of CPU time, requires 2 cores and 16 GB of RAM). We strongly discourage from running this inside a VM.
    • make setup-subset: Reproduce the results on a representative subset of our tasks (takes ~1 day of CPU time).
    • make setup-test: Smoke test the VM and the setup (takes ~15 min).
  2. Run make all-verification to run the verification of all the tools with all their configurations. In case you want to use the paper results execute cp -r results-paper results instead of running the experiments.
  3. Run make analyze-results to process the produced results in order to get human-readable results. They can be found in the results/tables directory. The CSV files used to generate the plots in the paper can be found in the output directory.

Environment

To run the artifact BenchExec, Python >= 3.12, and Java >= 21 are required.

Inside a clean VM running Ubuntu 24.04, please see the documentation of the respective tools for installation hints. A non-exhaustive list of required packages: * CPAchecker: Java 21 * SvLibChecker: Python >= 3.12

We recommend running the artifact inside the TACAS 26 VM,

Note that both MathSAT and Z3 which are used as SMT solvers inside the tools have been compiled for x86 architecture, and may not work for platforms other than the ones they were compiled for. In case such a problem is encountered, please execute make -B lib/pip inside the tools/svlibchecker directory to recompile MathSAT and Z3 for your architecture.

NOTE: We assume that all the following commands are executed from inside the root directory of the artifact!

Experiments

Setup

Run source benchmark-utils/local_config.sh (needs to be repeated every time a new shell is opened).

Benchmark Selection

Depending on your available resources you can select different sets of benchmarks to execute the tools on. You have the following options:

  • A quick test with two files, which can be useful to test that the artifact is behaving as intended. To select it use make setup-test. Executing this benchmark set should take ~15 minutes.
  • A subset of the tasks used for the benchmarks in the paper. To select it use make setup-subset. Executing this benchmark set should take around 1 day.
  • The full benchmark set used in the experiments. To select it use make setup-benchmark. Executing this benchmark set will take around 15 days of CPU Time.

Running the Experiments

To run all experiments multiple targets need to be executed one after the other, their list and order can be found in the TL;DR. Each of them encompass multiple targets for the different verifier configurations.

All experiments are run using BenchExec in order to ensure reliable benchmarks.

Smoke Test

To run the smoketest, just follow the instruction in the TL;DR using the test set, which can be configured using make setup-test.

Smoke Test Results

After running the target make all-verification for the test-set, the output on the command line should be similar to the one provided under doc/smoketest-cli-output.txt.

Results

The results contain not only the results from the paper, but also additional experiments done with different SMT-Solvers. The SMT-Solver for SvLibChecker is added as a suffix, either *-msat or *-z3 to indicate whether MathSAT or Z3 was used.

Generating the Results

Once you ran all experiments execute make analyze-results to generate an HTML table which contains the information used for the first three claims. It can be found in the results-paper/tables directory, and contains the results for all tools and configurations. For further information on how to interact with the HTML table, we refer to the BenchExec documentation. The numbers in the table and the quantile plots correspond to those in the paper. Each row in the table corresponds to a task, and each column corresponds to a tool configuration. The cells are colored according to the result of the tool on the task, and they contain the CPU time taken by the tool to solve the task.

The command make analyze-results also generates CSV files, and latex macros which can be used to generate the plots and tables in the paper. These are exported into the results directly of the data-analysis directory. We export a lot of different values in the macros file to make it easier to keep the paper up to date with the results, while the CSV files mostly contain the CPU time taken by each tool on each task, to produce the quantile plots for Claim 2. In addition, the information for Claim 3 is contained in the CSV file data-analysis/cache/cloc_results.csv, which contains the data generated by CLOC counting the LOC of the project.

Note that the processing of the *.xml.bz2 results into CSV files are cached during the data processing under data-analysis/cache, in order to make the development of the data-analysis easier. So if you want to re-process the results, you will need to delete the cache files first.

Analyzing the Results

The easiest way to compare the results with those in the paper is to make a diff of the generated tex macros file from the data analysis, and compare the quantile plots in the generated HTML table with the one from the paper. This only works if the full benchmark set is executed, since for the subset and the test-set the diff will contain a lot of differences. This can easily be done by executing:

diff -u data-analysis/output/tex-macros.tex results-paper/results/tex-macros.tex

In case you want to manually analyze the differences, the easiest way to do this for the Claims 1, and 2 is to interact with the generated HTML table. Each row contains the results for a task, and each column contains the results for a tool configuration. The name of the tool configurations and the ones from the paper are the same so you can easily find the ones you are interested in. For example, the columns name svlibchecker-predicate-analysis.correct-tags corresponds to the configuration of SvLibChecker with predicate abstraction, and the column cpachecker-predicate-analysis.correct-tags corresponds to the configuration of CPAchecker with predicate abstraction. * For Claim 1 you can check the numbers in the summary tab of the table, where you only need to look at the amount of correct and incorrect results for each tool configuration. For the amount of unique solved tasks you will need to check the macros generated in the data-analysis/results/tex-macros.tex file which contains them. * For Claim 2, you can check the quantile plots for each tool configuration in the HTML table, which is provided in the Quantile PLot tab of the table and should look something like the one from the paper results.

Information for Reuse

For developing and reusing this artifact for other purposes please look at developing.md.

In case you are interested in knowing more about the data-analysis we recommend looking at the README.md for the data-analysis directory.

Running the Tools on a single task

To know how to run the tools on a single task we recommend looking at the logfiles generated by BenchExec under results/$TOOL_NAME.*.logfiles.zip. Since this is always kept up-to-date with the commands used to run the tools, it is the best source of information to know how to run the tools on a single task. However, if you want to do this manually you can try running the following commands:

For SvLibChecker with predicate abstraction:

./tools/svlibchecker/svlibchecker.py --config tools/svlibchecker/config/predicateAnalysisCegar.toml ./tools/svlibchecker/examples/loop-simple.unsafe.svlib
# Should produce: `Verification result: incorrect`

For CPAchecker with predicate abstraction:

./tools/cpachecker/bin/cpachecker --config ./tools/cpachecker/config/predicateAnalysis-svlib.properties  ./tools/svlibchecker/examples/loop-simple.unsafe.svlib
# Should produce: `Verification result: FALSE`

Increasing the parallelism to run the Artifact Locally

If you want to run the artifact locally and have more resources available, than only 16 GB of memory and 3 cores, you can increase the parallelism of the execution of the artifact by changing -N 1 in local_config.sh to a higher number, for example -N 4 to run 4 processes in parallel. Increasing the amount of processes will also increase the amount of memory, and CPU cores required to run the artifact, since each process requires 2 cores and 15 GB of memory, so make sure to have enough resources available before increasing the parallelism.

Debugging the Artifact

If you encounter any exception or error during the execution of the smoketest, we recommend the following steps to try and solve the problem: * Figure out if the error is caused by running the tools or by missing dependencies. If BenchExec could not start, it is likely that the error is caused by missing dependencies or by a misconfiguration of the environment. * In case the error is caused by missing dependencies or by a misconfiguration of the environment, we recommend checking the output of the setup_vm.sh script and the local_config.sh file in the benchmark-utils directory to check if all dependencies are installed and if the environment is set up correctly. * In case the error is caused by the tools, we recommend checking the logs of the tools under results/$TOOL_NAME.*.logfiles.zip, and running the command-line in the first line of the logfile for further debugging.

Known Issues

Warnings

Overheating

During the execution of the experiments, a warning may appear which tells us that the CPU was throttled due to overheating. This affects the time measurements in the results, but should not happen when reproducing the results outside a VM.

2024-XX-XX XX:XX:XX - WARNING - CPU throttled itself during benchmarking due to overheating. Benchmark results are unreliable!

Overlayfs

During the execution of the experiments, a warning may appear which tells us that the home directory should be given as an overlay or hidden. Currently it is not possible to do neither of those inside the TACAS23 VM due to its old overlayfs and due to not knowing the path to the folder where the artifact is being executed.

2024-XX-XX XX:XX:XX - WARNING - Home directory in container should be /home/benchexec but this directory cannot be created due to directory mode of parent directory. It is recommended to use '--overlay-dir /home' or '--hidden-dir /home' and overwrite directory modes for subdirectories where necessary.

Resource Requirements

During the execution of the experiments, a warning may appear which tells us that the resource requirements are being ignored. This only means that the resource requirements regarding CPU model are being ignored, this has no effect on the benchmarking.

Errors

Overlay

When BenchExec tries to create an overlay mount while there is a shared folder mounted inside the VM, the following error may occur:

2024-XX-XX XX:XX:XX - ERROR - Failed to create overlay mount for /home/...: invalid argument ...

In this case, the shared folder should be unmounted and the experiments should be run again.

C Groups

If BenchExec is unable to use C groups to benchmark then a restart of the VM may help make BenchExec work as intended.

Unprivileged User Namespaces

If BenchExec provides the following error:

2025-10-24 09:54:59 - WARNING - Creating UID mapping into container failed: [Errno 1] Operation not permitted
2025-10-24 09:54:59 - WARNING - Could not write to setgroups file in /proc: [Errno 13] Permission denied: '/proc/3078/setgroups'
2025-10-24 09:54:59 - WARNING - Creating GID mapping into container failed: [Errno 1] Operation not permitted
Error: Unprivileged user namespaces forbidden on this system, please enable them with 'sysctl -w kernel.apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns=0'. Ubuntu disables them by default since 24.04, refer to https://ubuntu.com/blog/ubuntu-23-10-restricted-unprivileged-user-namespaces for more information.

The you need to execute the following, for everything to work as intended:

sudo sysctl -w kernel.apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns=0

Missing CPU Instructions

Sometimes the smoketest will throw exceptions for all/most tasks, since it cannot run the SMT-Solvers in the backend. In such a case it is likely that they were compiled for a different CPU model, than the one being used to run the experiments. In such a case, we recommend re-building the tools such that the SMT-Solvers are compiled for the specific CPU model of the machine. This can easly be done by running:

make -B tools/svlibchecker tools/cpachecker

Note: It may only be necessary to re-build one of the tools.

metadata.title: lab-i40/LLM-as-a-Decision-Making-Core-for-Semantic-Capability-Check: v1.0.0
metadata.description:
This is the initial public release of the reproduction package for the paper "Large Language Models as a Decision-making Core for Semantic Capability Check in Asset Administration Shell-based Intelligent Manufacturing."

Capability Check module (src/capability_check.py) — implements the core algorithm that receives a provider and a requester AAS capability submodel, preprocesses them (stripping non-English descriptions, qualifiers, semantic IDs, and model type metadata), renders the system and user prompts, and calls the LLM via an OpenAI-compatible API. Returns a structured result with the capable decision, the model's justification, token usage, and the raw output.

Test suite (tests/) — four test groups (G1–G4) covering 454 balanced positive/negative cases for semantic capability matching, insufficient inferential evidence, limiting properties and parameterization, and invalid or inconsistent data. Each group is parametrized from the corresponding dataset file. The conftest.py integrates with pytest-repeat and pytest-xdist, collecting per-test results and writing timestamped JSON reports, a text summary, and a cumulative benchmark history CSV at the end of each session.

Dataset (dataset/) — four JSON files containing the full test case corpus derived from Screwing capability submodel instances, with base instances built in AASX Package Explorer and extended through automated parametric variation and manual structural editing.

Prompts (prompts/) — system and user prompt templates used by the capability check module, with placeholders for the provider and requester submodels.

metadata.title: 'MelT: Reproduction package for 'A Portable, Single-GEMM Mel Audio Frontend via Non-Uniform DFT'
metadata.description:
Reproduction package for the paper "MelT: A Portable, Single-GEMM Mel Audio Frontend via Non-Uniform DFT with Measured Latency and Energy Gains on GPUs" (A. Camargo and M. Finger).

MelT re-casts the conventional STFT → power → Mel pipeline as a single dense matrix multiplication (a Mel-spaced NDFT projection), so the audio frontend runs on the same GEMM substrate that modern accelerators already optimize. This package contains the MelT/MFCCT implementation, config-driven experiment runners, and an analysis pipeline that regenerates every table and figure in the paper from raw measurements (make paper), together with the aggregated results.

Contents. Installable library (src/melt/); per-platform benchmark runners for latency, energy (directly-measured NVML/powermetrics), external-library baselines, Mel-bin sweep, batch scaling, and the V100 roofline; downstream task harnesses (frozen-Whisper WER equivalence, SPIRA clinical classification, VoxCeleb speaker attributes, feature-level equivalence) with full statistics (TOST, McNemar, DeLong, Wilcoxon, bootstrap CIs, multi-seed); a manifest mapping each paper float to the exact command that produces it; and a preflight checker.

Hardware. Evaluated on NVIDIA H100 and V100, and Apple M4 Pro and A18 Pro.

Data. No audio is bundled. The LibriSpeech-derived Libri6000 corpus is rebuilt byte-for-byte from public LibriSpeech train-clean-100 (OpenSLR SLR12, CC-BY 4.0) via data/build_libri_100_160.py (recipe + sha256 checksums included). VoxCeleb1 and SPIRA are obtained from their official sources (license-restricted; not re-hosted).

License. Code: MIT. Figures and CSV artifacts: CC-BY 4.0.
